item.title: Akasaki Pottery Village: Tottori's Folk Ceramics — Guide
item.description: The Akasaki area near Hokuei is one of the centres of Tottori’s folk-pottery tradition, closely tied to the Mingei (folk craft) movement that flourished in the region in the twentieth century. Local kilns produce sturdy, unpretentious everyday ceramics — plates, bowls, teapots and jars in earthy glazes of amber, green and black, designed to be used rather than admired. Studios and shops in the area let visitors browse and buy directly from potters, see the kilns and, at some, try their hand at the wheel.

item.title: Bizen Pottery: Unglazed Stoneware from Japan's Oldest Kilns — Guide
item.description: Bizen ware is among the oldest continuously produced ceramics in Japan, one of the Six Ancient Kilns, fired in the town of Imbe for roughly a thousand years. Its defining trait is refusal: no glaze is applied at all. Instead the local iron-rich clay is fired for up to two weeks in wood-burning kilns, where ash, flame and the position of each piece produce the russet reds, scorch marks, and sesame-seed speckles that make every piece unique.

item.title: Hagi Ware: Pottery and Hands-On Workshops — Guide
item.description: Hagi ware, or Hagi-yaki, is among the most esteemed pottery in Japan, traditionally ranked second only to Raku among wares favoured for the tea ceremony. Made in the castle town of Hagi for over four hundred years, it is prized not for bold decoration but for quiet, understated beauty: soft cream and pinkish glazes, a warm translucent surface, and a character that changes subtly over years of use as tea seeps into the fine crackle.

item.title: Karatsu Ware: Rustic Pottery for Tea — Guide
item.description: While much of Saga is famous for refined white porcelain, the town of Karatsu is home to a very different ceramic tradition: Karatsu-yaki, a rustic, earthy stoneware. Made here for over 400 years, Karatsu ware is prized for its warm, understated, unpretentious beauty — muted earth tones, simple forms, natural ash and iron glazes, and a rough texture that changes and deepens with use. It has long been especially valued for the tea ceremony, so much so that connoisseurs traditionally rank tea bowls as ‘first Raku, second Hagi, third Karatsu’.

item.title: Tamba-yaki: 800 Years of Unglazed Stoneware — Guide
item.description: Tamba-yaki is one of the Six Ancient Kilns of Japan, the handful of pottery centres that have fired continuously since the medieval period, and its kilns have been working in the hills of Tamba-Sasayama for roughly 800 years. The style is defined by what it refuses to add: no applied glaze, the surfaces instead coloured by wood ash falling on the clay in long climbing-kiln firings, producing greens, browns and glassy runs no two of which are alike.

item.title: Akahada Ware: Nara's Tea-Ceremony Pottery — Guide
item.description: Akahada ware (Akahada-yaki) is the traditional pottery of Nara, made for centuries at kilns on the slopes of Mount Akahada near Yamatokoriyama. Counted among the celebrated ‘Enshu Seven Kilns’ favoured by tea masters, it is a warm, understated stoneware with a soft cream or reddish glaze, prized for tea-ceremony bowls and vessels. A distinctive local style decorates the pieces with ‘Nara-e’ — charming hand-painted pictures of Nara’s deer, Buddhist figures and landscapes — giving the ware a gentle, storytelling character.

item.title: Echizen Pottery: One of Japan's Six Ancient Kilns — Guide
item.description: Echizen ware is one of Japan’s Six Ancient Kilns, the country’s most historically significant pottery-producing centres, with a ceramic tradition in the region spanning some 850 years, known for its unglazed, earthy, high-fired stoneware whose natural ash-glaze finishes develop during wood firing. Today the Echizen pottery area gathers kilns, galleries and a ceramic museum, and workshops let visitors try the potter’s wheel or hand-forming themselves under artisan guidance, shaping a piece to be fired and sent on later.

item.title: Yachimun Pottery Guide: Tsuboya Street & Workshops (Naha)
item.description: Yachimun is the Okinawan word for pottery, and the island’s bold, earthy ceramics are among its most beloved crafts. The heart of the tradition is Tsuboya, a historic pottery quarter just off Kokusai-dori in Naha, where a charming stone-paved lane is lined with kilns, studios, galleries and shops. Here you’ll find rustic plates and cups, awamori flasks, and the famous shisa lion-dog guardians. Browsing the lane — or trying the wheel yourself — is a lovely, low-key cultural break in the city.

item.title: Okayama Leisure Guide: Kibiji Cycling, Pottery Workshops & Canal Cruises
item.description: Okayama sits at the midpoint of Japan’s Sanyo corridor, a city most visitors pass through on the Shinkansen rather than stop in. That habit overlooks one of western Japan’s most satisfying combinations of leisure: a canal-side cycling trail lined with ancient history, a 1,000-year-old pottery tradition still fired in working kilns, and a preserved Edo-period merchant town that rewards an afternoon of unhurried walking and a slow boat on a willow-fringed canal.

item.title: Shiga Leisure Guide: Lake Biwa Cycling, Ninja Villages & Pottery
item.description: Shiga Prefecture operates at a pace that suits unhurried exploration. The prefecture’s defining feature — Lake Biwa, Japan’s largest lake, occupying a full sixth of the prefecture’s area — provides a natural organizing axis for a day of activity. You can cycle sections of its shoreline in the morning, cruise across its surface in the afternoon, and eat Omi beef sukiyaki in the evening. Alternatively, the hills southeast of the lake lead to a ninja heritage site and a pottery village whose traditions predate most of what Kyoto’s tourists queue for.

item.title: Tochigi Girls' Trip: Onsen, Pottery, Strawberries & Nikko
item.description: Tochigi Prefecture sits just 90 minutes north of Tokyo yet feels worlds apart — mountain air, hot spring rivers, ancient cedar forests, and a craftwork tradition that has endured for centuries. For a group of women looking for a trip that blends relaxation, creativity, good food, and a little culture, it checks nearly every box. Onsen ryokan in Kinugawa, hand-throwing pottery in Mashiko, strawberry farms outside Utsunomiya, artisan cheese in Nasu’s highlands, and the gold-gilded shrines of Nikko make for a three-day itinerary that feels genuinely varied without being exhausting.
